claims.text: Increasing silicon content in CrFeCoNiX alloys promotes formation of a coherent, silica-enriched oxide layer.
The silica-enriched oxide layer remains stable during exposure above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
CrFeCoNiX alloys with low silicon content form mixed oxides that crack or spall.
CrFeCoNiX alloys containing higher amounts of Mn or Al form mixed oxides that crack or spall.
Silicon preferentially forms a protective silica-based oxide in CrFeCoNiX alloys.
The proposed silica-based oxide has lower internal stress than heterogeneous oxide scales formed when Mn or Al predominate with the base metals.
The proposed silica-based oxide adheres better than heterogeneous oxide scales formed when Mn or Al predominate with the base metals.
Increasing silicon content improves oxide-scale coherence under high-temperature oxidative conditions.
Increasing silicon content improves oxide-scale adhesion and resistance to cracking or spallation relative to otherwise comparable low-silicon alloys.
The hypothesis applies to single-phase metallic solid solutions of CrFeCoNiX.
The proposed behavior applies during long-term exposure exceeding 100 hours at temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative atmospheres.
Prior studies support a mechanistic role for silicon in promoting protective oxide formation.
The effects of interactions between silicon and Mn or Al in multiphase systems remain uncertain.
Failure of the high-silicon alloy to show significantly better coherence, adhesion, and cracking or spallation resistance than the low-silicon control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated boundary requires exposure longer than 100 hours, but the proposed falsification experiment uses exactly 100 hours and therefore falls outside that boundary.
The conditions claim applicability in an oxidative and corrosive environment, whereas the boundary limits applicability to oxidative atmospheres and does not define coverage of corrosive atmospheres.
